stem: What is the piezoelectric effect?

options.content: the production of a p.d. across a crystal when it is mechanically stressed
options.rationale: Correct (and the converse: a p.d. changes its shape).

options.content: the reflection of ultrasound at a boundary between two media
options.rationale: Reflection depends on acoustic impedance, not on piezoelectricity.

options.content: the heating of a crystal when an alternating current is passed through it for some time
options.rationale: This is just resistive heating.

options.content: the emission of electrons from a crystal when ultrasound falls on it
options.rationale: Ultrasound does not eject electrons.

explanation: Stress produces a p.d. (detection); a p.d. produces a change of shape (generation).

stem: Why is a gel applied between an ultrasound transducer and the patient's skin?

options.content: To exclude air, so that very little ultrasound is reflected at the skin.
options.rationale: Correct: air has a tiny Z compared with skin.

options.content: To cool the skin, which is heated by the ultrasound.
options.rationale: Diagnostic ultrasound causes negligible heating.

options.content: To absorb unwanted echoes from inside the body.
options.rationale: The gel transmits ultrasound; it does not absorb echoes.

options.content: To increase the frequency of the ultrasound that enters the patient's body through the skin.
options.rationale: Frequency is set by the transducer, not the gel.

explanation: Without gel, the air gap's impedance mismatch reflects about 99.9% of the intensity; the gel matches the skin's impedance.

stem: Blood has a density of $1040\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$ and the speed of sound in it is $1570\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. What is its specific acoustic impedance?

options.rationale: Z is the product, not the ratio, of c and ρ.
Correct: Z = ρc.
Z is ρ multiplied by c.
This is ρc², not ρc.

stem: Which pair of media gives the largest intensity reflection coefficient at their boundary?

options.content: fat and muscle
options.rationale: Their impedances are similar, so little is reflected.

options.content: air and soft tissue
options.rationale: Correct: the largest impedance mismatch (about 4 × 10² against 1.6 × 10⁶).

options.content: blood and soft tissue
options.rationale: Almost identical impedances.

options.content: coupling gel and skin
options.rationale: The gel is chosen to match the skin.

explanation: I_R/I₀ depends on (Z₁ − Z₂)²/(Z₁ + Z₂)², largest when the impedances are most different.

stem: How is the same piezoelectric transducer able both to send and to receive ultrasound pulses?

options.content: It emits continuously and filters out its own signal to leave the echoes.
options.rationale: Pulse-echo needs separate emission and listening periods.

options.content: Half the crystal emits while the other half receives.
options.rationale: One crystal does both, at different times.

options.content: The returning echoes reverse the current in the crystal, which then switches it back to emitting mode.
options.rationale: Echoes produce a small p.d.; they do not switch the mode.

options.content: It emits a short pulse, then acts as a receiver, producing a p.d. when echoes deform the crystal.
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: Pulse, then listen: the reverse piezoelectric effect generates, the direct effect detects.
hints: The pulses are short and the gaps between them are long.

stem: An echo is received $104\ \mu\text{s}$ after a pulse is emitted into soft tissue, where the speed of sound is $1540\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. How deep is the reflecting boundary?

options.rationale: This is the total distance there and back.
Divide the round trip by 2, not 4.
330 m s⁻¹ is the speed of sound in air, not tissue.
Correct: d = ct/2.

hints: The pulse goes to the boundary and back.

stem: Why is a higher ultrasound frequency used to image structures close to the skin than to image deep organs?

options.content: Higher frequencies travel faster, so their echoes return sooner.
options.rationale: The speed in tissue is nearly independent of frequency.

options.content: Higher frequencies are reflected less at tissue boundaries, so more of each pulse reaches the shallow organs.
options.rationale: Reflection depends on impedances, not frequency.

options.content: Higher frequencies give finer detail but are attenuated more, so they do not penetrate as far.
options.rationale: Correct: a trade-off between resolution and depth.

options.content: Lower frequencies cannot be produced by small transducers.
options.rationale: Transducer size is not the reason.

explanation: Shorter wavelength resolves smaller details, but μ increases with frequency, limiting depth.
hints: Think about wavelength and about attenuation.

stem: An ultrasound beam passes from muscle into bone. Which statement explains why structures behind bone are hard to image?

options.content: Bone has a lower acoustic impedance than muscle, so the ultrasound speeds up inside it and its energy is lost to the surroundings.
options.rationale: Bone has a much higher impedance.

options.content: Ultrasound cannot travel through solids.
options.rationale: Sound travels well through solids; the problem is reflection and attenuation.

options.content: A large fraction is reflected at the boundary and bone attenuates strongly, so little reaches beyond it.
options.rationale: Correct: impedance mismatch plus high attenuation.

options.content: The echoes from behind bone return too quickly to be detected.
options.rationale: Echoes from deeper structures take longer, not less time.

explanation: Muscle-bone reflects about 40% of the intensity and bone attenuates strongly, casting an acoustic shadow.
hints: Compare the impedances of muscle and bone.

stem: Fat has an acoustic impedance of $1.35 \times 10^{6}\ \text{kg m}^{-2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ and kidney tissue $1.62 \times 10^{6}\ \text{kg m}^{-2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$. Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient at the boundary, to two significant figures.
explanation: $\dfrac{I_R}{I_0} = \dfrac{(1.62 - 1.35)^2}{(1.62 + 1.35)^2} = \dfrac{0.0729}{8.82} = 8.3 \times 10^{-3}$. Forgetting to square gives the amplitude ratio, not the intensity ratio.
workedSolution: 1. $\dfrac{I_R}{I_0} = \dfrac{(1.62 - 1.35)^2}{(1.62 + 1.35)^2} = \dfrac{0.0729}{8.82} = 8.3 \times 10^{-3}$. Forgetting to square gives the amplitude ratio, not the intensity ratio.
hints: Square both the difference and the sum.

stem: Ultrasound of a certain frequency has an attenuation coefficient of $70\ \text{m}^{-1}$ in muscle. Calculate the fraction of the intensity remaining after it has travelled $3.0\ \text{cm}$ through muscle, to two significant figures.
explanation: $I/I_0 = e^{-\mu x} = e^{-70 \times 0.030} = e^{-2.1} = 0.12$. Leaving $x$ in cm gives a meaningless tiny value.
workedSolution: 1. $I/I_0 = e^{-\mu x} = e^{-70 \times 0.030} = e^{-2.1} = 0.12$. Leaving $x$ in cm gives a meaningless tiny value.

stem: An ultrasound beam's intensity falls from $0.50\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ to $0.20\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ in passing through $2.5\ \text{cm}$ of tissue. Calculate the attenuation coefficient, in $\text{m}^{-1}$, to two significant figures.
explanation:
1. $I = I_0e^{-\mu x} \Rightarrow \mu = \dfrac{\ln(I_0/I)}{x}$.
2. $\mu = \dfrac{\ln(0.50/0.20)}{0.025} = \dfrac{0.916}{0.025} = 37\ \text{m}^{-1}$.
3. Using lg instead of ln, or x in cm, are the usual errors.
workedSolution:
1. 1. $I = I_0e^{-\mu x} \Rightarrow \mu = \dfrac{\ln(I_0/I)}{x}$.
2. $\mu = \dfrac{\ln(0.50/0.20)}{0.025} = \dfrac{0.916}{0.025} = 37\ \text{m}^{-1}$.
3. Using lg instead of ln, or x in cm, are the usual errors.

stem: A pulse enters soft tissue (attenuation coefficient $55\ \text{m}^{-1}$) and is reflected at a boundary $4.0\ \text{cm}$ below the skin, where the intensity reflection coefficient is $0.012$. Calculate the intensity of the echo arriving back at the skin as a fraction of the intensity that entered, to two significant figures. Assume no other losses.
explanation:
1. The pulse travels $4.0\ \text{cm}$ down and $4.0\ \text{cm}$ back: $x = 0.080\ \text{m}$.
2. Attenuation over the round trip: $e^{-55 \times 0.080} = 0.0123$.
3. Fraction returning $= 0.012 \times 0.0123 = 1.5 \times 10^{-4}$. This is why the scanner amplifies late (deep) echoes more.
workedSolution:
1. 1. The pulse travels $4.0\ \text{cm}$ down and $4.0\ \text{cm}$ back: $x = 0.080\ \text{m}$.
2. Attenuation over the round trip: $e^{-55 \times 0.080} = 0.0123$.
3. Fraction returning $= 0.012 \times 0.0123 = 1.5 \times 10^{-4}$. This is why the scanner amplifies late (deep) echoes more.
hints: The pulse is attenuated on the way down and on the way back.

stem: In an A-scan of an eye, echoes from the front and back of the lens arrive $42\ \mu\text{s}$ and $97\ \mu\text{s}$ after the pulse. Taking the speed of sound as $1540\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, calculate the thickness of the lens, in mm, to two significant figures.
explanation:
1. Time difference $= 97 - 42 = 55\ \mu\text{s}$ for the extra round trip through the lens.
2. Thickness $= \dfrac{1540 \times 55 \times 10^{-6}}{2} = 42\ \text{mm}$. (Sound travels faster in the lens than in watery tissue, so this is an estimate.)
workedSolution:
1. 1. Time difference $= 97 - 42 = 55\ \mu\text{s}$ for the extra round trip through the lens.
2. Thickness $= \dfrac{1540 \times 55 \times 10^{-6}}{2} = 42\ \text{mm}$. (Sound travels faster in the lens than in watery tissue, so this is an estimate.)
hints: Use the difference between the two echo times.

stem: The depth of a boundary is found from $d = ct/2$ with $t = 64 \pm 2\ \mu\text{s}$ and $c = 1540 \pm 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in $d$, to two significant figures.
explanation: $\%d = \%t + \%c = \dfrac{2}{64} \times 100 + \dfrac{20}{1540} \times 100 = 3.1 + 1.3 = 4.4\%$ (the factor ½ is exact).
hints: Percentage uncertainties add for a product.

stem: Ultrasound is preferred to X-rays for routine imaging of a fetus because, at diagnostic intensities, it is not ionising.
explanation: True. Ultrasound is a mechanical wave and does not ionise atoms, so it carries no known risk at diagnostic intensities.

stem: Match each quantity with its unit.
explanation: Z = ρc: kg m⁻³ × m s⁻¹; μ in m⁻¹; intensity in W m⁻²; I_R/I₀ is a ratio.

stem: Complete the statements.

payload.template: Ultrasound is produced when an alternating {{blank:a}} is applied to a piezoelectric crystal, making it vibrate at its {{blank:b}} frequency. The fraction of intensity reflected at a boundary depends on the difference in acoustic {{blank:c}} of the two media.

explanation: Alternating p.d. → vibration at resonance; reflection depends on Z₁ and Z₂.

stem: Explain how a piezoelectric transducer is used to produce an ultrasound image of a boundary inside the body.

points.description: An alternating p.d. (at the crystal's resonant frequency) makes the crystal vibrate, emitting a short pulse of ultrasound into the body (through gel).
The pulse is partly reflected at boundaries between tissues with different acoustic impedances.
The returning echo makes the crystal vibrate, producing a p.d. that is amplified and detected (the transducer acts as a receiver between pulses).
The time delay gives the depth (d = ct/2) and the echo strength gives information about the boundary; sweeping the beam builds an image (B-scan).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: An alternating p.d. at the crystal's resonant frequency makes it vibrate and send a short ultrasound pulse into the body through a coupling gel. At each boundary between tissues of different acoustic impedance part of the pulse is reflected. Between pulses the transducer listens: an echo deforms the crystal, producing a small p.d. that is amplified. The delay gives the depth of the boundary, d = ct/2, and its size gives information about the boundary; sweeping the beam across the body builds a two-dimensional image.

explanation: Generate, reflect, detect, time.
hints: Describe both uses of the crystal.

stem: Explain, with reference to acoustic impedance, why almost no ultrasound enters the body if the gel is not used.

points.description: Without gel, air is trapped between the transducer and the skin.
Air's acoustic impedance (about 400 kg m⁻² s⁻¹) is very much smaller than that of skin (about 1.6 × 10⁶).
So the intensity reflection coefficient is almost 1 (about 0.999): nearly all the ultrasound is reflected at the air-skin boundary.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Without gel there is a layer of air between the probe and the skin. The impedance of air is about four thousand times smaller than that of skin, so (Z₁ − Z₂)²/(Z₁ + Z₂)² is about 0.999 and almost all the ultrasound is reflected at the boundary.

explanation: Large mismatch, near-total reflection.
hints: Compare Z for air and for skin.

stem: Define specific acoustic impedance and state how the intensity reflected at a boundary depends on it.

points.description: Z = density × speed of sound in the medium (ρc).
The larger the difference between the impedances of the two media, the larger the fraction reflected: I_R/I₀ = (Z₁ − Z₂)²/(Z₁ + Z₂)².

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Specific acoustic impedance is the product of the density of a medium and the speed of sound in it, Z = ρc. The fraction of intensity reflected at a boundary is (Z₁ − Z₂)²/(Z₁ + Z₂)², so it is large when the impedances are very different.

explanation: Z = ρc.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the missing value of ln(I/I₀), to three decimal places. Include the sign.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why a graph of ln(I/I₀) against x should be a straight line through the origin, and how μ is found from it.

points.description: $I = I_0e^{-\mu x} \Rightarrow \ln(I/I_0) = -\mu x$: the form $y = mx$.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Since $I/I_0 = e^{-\mu x}$, $\ln(I/I_0) = -\mu x$, a straight line through the origin with gradient $-\mu$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Determine the attenuation coefficient $\mu$, in $\text{m}^{-1}$, to two significant figures.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Use your value of μ to calculate the thickness of gel that halves the intensity, in cm, to two significant figures.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest two precautions to make the readings reliable.

points.description: Use gel between the transducers and each slab (no air gaps), and the same pressure/contact each time.
Keep the frequency, transducer separation/alignment and output constant; repeat each reading and average.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Couple the transducers to each slab with gel so there is no air, using the same contact pressure, and keep the frequency, alignment and output power the same; repeat and average each reading.

explanation: ln(I/I₀) = −μx: gradient −μ; half-thickness ln 2/μ.
hints: Take natural logs of I = I₀e^(−μx).

stem: An ultrasound pulse passes through a layer of fat into muscle and then meets bone. Acoustic impedances (in $\text{kg m}^{-2}\ \text{s}^{-1}$): fat $1.38 \times 10^{6}$, muscle $1.70 \times 10^{6}$, bone $7.80 \times 10^{6}$. Ignore attenuation.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the fraction of the incident intensity reflected at the fat-muscle boundary, to two significant figures.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the fraction reflected at the muscle-bone boundary, to two significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Use your answers to explain why ultrasound gives clear images of soft-tissue boundaries but cannot image the inside of bones well.

points.description: Soft-tissue boundaries reflect only a small fraction (about 1%), so most of the pulse continues to deeper boundaries and produces echoes from each.
At bone about 40% is reflected (and bone attenuates strongly), so little ultrasound enters the bone and structures behind it are in shadow.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Only about 1% is reflected at a fat-muscle boundary, so most of the pulse travels on and every deeper soft-tissue boundary returns an echo. At bone about 41% is reflected, and bone also absorbs strongly, so little ultrasound penetrates it.

explanation: I_R/I₀ = (Z₁ − Z₂)²/(Z₁ + Z₂)²; small mismatches allow deep imaging.
